method: A single sharp obstruction is reduced to the Fresnel–Kirchhoff parameter v = h × √(2/λ × (1/d1 + 1/d2)), where h is the obstruction height above the straight line between the antennas in metres and d1 and d2 are the two leg lengths in metres. The diffraction loss follows the ITU-R P.526 single-edge approximation L = 6.9 + 20 log10(√((v − 0.1)² + 1) + v − 0.1) dB, which gives 6.03 dB when the edge grazes the line at v = 0, and is taken as zero once v is at or below −0.78, so an edge that clears the path adds no loss instead of a small gain. The first Fresnel radius at the obstruction is r1 = √(λ d1 d2/(d1 + d2)) and the clearance is reported as −h/r1, which equals −v/√2; a positive clearance means the edge sits below the line. The free-space loss 20 log10(4π(d1 + d2)/λ) over the whole path is reported alongside the diffraction loss and their sum. Wavelength is λ = c/f with c = 299,792,458 m/s exactly, so 2400 MHz gives 0.1249 m. Values are refused outside 1 to 100,000 MHz for frequency, 0.01 to 500 km for each leg and −1000 to 1000 m for the edge height, and decimal commas are accepted. The page models one sharp edge over flat ground with no atmosphere, terrain profile, rounded-ridge correction, multiple edges, vegetation or ground reflection, it does not recommend antenna heights or judge whether a link will close, and it runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: A single knife-edge obstruction is characterised by the Fresnel–Kirchhoff diffraction parameter v, which grows with the obstruction height above the line of sight and with the square root of 2/λ × (1/d1 + 1/d2).
ITU-R P.526 approximates the loss of a single knife edge as 6.9 + 20 log10(√((v − 0.1)² + 1) + v − 0.1) dB, about 6 dB at grazing incidence, and treats edges well below the line as no loss.
The first Fresnel zone radius at the obstruction is √(λ d1 d2/(d1 + d2)), so clearance is commonly judged against that radius rather than against the geometric line alone.
